study.title: Ezekiel 1 The inaugural vision of the glory of the LORD
study.overview: Ezekiel receives his prophetic vocation in the midst of the exiles, not in Jerusalem, but in the land of the Chaldeans, by the river Chebar. The vision presents the glory of the LORD in highly symbolic language: stormy wind, fire, living beings, wheels and a throne. The chapter prepares the reader for the main message of the book: the holy God rules history, judges the sin of his people, but does not abandon his promise. The reaction of the prophet, falling on the face, shows that divine revelation is not spectacle, but encounter that humiliates and commissions.

outline.title: Called in the midst of exile
outline.explanation: The date, place and identity of Ezekiel are carefully registered. He is among the exiles, and it is there that the word of the LORD comes to him, confirming that his prophetic mission is born in the context of judgment, but also of divine presence.

outline.title: Living beings and the perfect movement
outline.explanation: The storm, fire, and the four living beings form a scene of majesty and order. Their faces, wings and displacement without hesitation communicate fullness, speed and obedience to the spirit that directs them.

outline.title: Fire, wheels and invisible government
outline.explanation: The movement of beings and wheels shows that God's action is not limited by place or obstacle. The wheels full of eyes and accompanied by the spirit reinforce the idea of attentive, vigilant and sovereign government over everything that happens.

outline.title: The throne, voice and glory of the Lord
outline.explanation: On the firmament appears the throne, and upon it a figure similar to a man. The brightness as a heavenly bow culminates in the identification of the vision as the likeness of the glory of the LORD; before it, Ezekiel falls down and hears the voice that speaks.

study.context: The text places the beginning of Ezekiel's ministry in the fifth year of the captivity of King Joachim, among the exiles taken to the land of the Chaldeans. The notes provided highlight that this occurs amidst the deported people, and that the prophetic call serves to legitimize the prophet's message as the word of the LORD. It is also indicated that the vision introduces the themes of the book, especially the imminent judgment on the people of God. There is no need for additional reconstructions other than what the chapter itself informs.
study.theology: Chapter theology combines holiness, sovereignty and hope. First, God reveals Himself as absolutely glorious and above the created world; the vision does not diminish its transcendence, but manifests it through unusual images. Second, the presence of the wheels, the coordinated movement and the eyes suggests that the divine government is active, attentive and impossible to be frustrated. Third, the bow in the clouds, according to the notes, adds a sign of mercy in the midst of the proclamation of judgment: destruction will not be the last word of God. Finally, the prophet's prostration shows that true revelation produces reverence, not light familiarity. Even when the vision is terrible, it also confirms that the Lord continues to speak to his people.

scholarViews.insight: The call of Ezekiel begins among the exiles and serves to authenticate his commission as messenger of the LORD, introducing from the beginning the theme of imminent judgment.
The glingor like a heavenly bow adds a note of mercy to the judgment scene, and Ezekiel's reaction to seeing the glory of the LORD is to fall on his face.
The wheels are connected to living beings, so that they advance with the same movement; this reinforces the idea of coordination and perfect government in the vision.

questions: Why does God choose to reveal his glory and call Ezekiel right in the midst of exile?
What does the image of the eye-filled wheels teach about how God rules history?
How does the mixture of judgment and hope in this chapter correct our expectations about the holiness of God?
study.practice: Read this chapter as a preparation to hear God reverently. If you go through a period of loss, remember that the LORD is not absent from exile: he continues to speak, rule and sustain his promise. Apply this by examining your response to God's presence: instead of treating revelation as curiosity, receive it with humility, repentance, and obedient attention. It is also worth remembering that the glory of God does not nullify his mercy; therefore, even in times of discipline, wait in him and remain faithful.
study.uncertainty: The chapter contains highly symbolic language and the given notes recognize interpretations in some details, such as the temporal reference of verse 1 and accurate understanding of certain images. It is not possible to affirm with absolute certainty the meaning of each visual element of the vision without overcoming what the text and notes allow. Nor should confessional readings be transformed into undisputed facts of the text.
